title: حِكَايَةُ قَمَرِ الزَّمَانِ
source: William Hay Macnaghten, ed., The Alif Laila, or Book of the Thousand Nights and One Night, vol. 1, Calcutta 1839 (“Calcutta II”), printed pp. 824–826 (Night 179, continuing nights-178), transcribed from the 300 ppi scan (archive.org aliflailaorbooko01macn) by the editors' own transcription. The edition prints the prose essentially unpointed: ALL VOCALIZATION (tashkīl) IS EDITORIAL — ours, not the edition's — and the alphabet button strips it back to the bare rasm as Macnaghten prints it, except where a clear misprint has been corrected (each is noted). Romanization is simplified IJMES. Spelling, including the edition’s Middle Arabic forms, is preserved; clear misprints are corrected in the text, and the note on each gives the print’s reading. Obscure or doubtful forms are kept as printed, vocalized by evident sense and flagged in the notes. Read-aloud audio is a Modern Standard Arabic reading of this vocalised text, synthesized by machine, with word-by-word timing generated the same way.
about: Night 179 continues the tale of Qamar al-Zamān. Dahnash finishes his account of the princess for Maymūna: her father, King al-Ghayūr, a tyrant and a fearless rider of battles, loves her so dearly that he has built her seven palaces, of crystal, marble, Chinese iron, precious stones, onyx and coloured stone, silver and gold, and she moves from one to the next through the year. Her name is Queen Budūr. When kings send to ask for her hand she refuses: she is a sovereign who rules, she says, and wants no man ruling over her; pressed again, she threatens to fall on a sword. Her father shuts her away under ten old stewardesses and gives out that she has gone mad. Dahnash confesses that he visits her every night to gaze at her and kiss her as she sleeps, and begs Maymūna to come and see her. Maymūna laughs, spits in his face and scorns the girl — then boasts of the youth she saw that night, imprisoned by his father in her own tower for refusing marriage, and calls Dahnash a liar for thinking anyone could match him. Dawn overtakes Shahrazād. As with every printed edition of the Nights, this one belongs to the late Egyptian recension (ZER) — an eighteenth-century expansion padded out to a literal 1001 nights; no printed edition is a medieval text, and Macnaghten regularised the language here and there, so some Middle Arabic texture is a nineteenth-century retrofit.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا كَانَتِ اللَّيْلَةُ التَّاسِعَةُ وَالسَّبْعُونَ بَعْدَ الْمِائَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā kānati al-laylatu al-tāsiʿatu wa-al-sabʿūna baʿda al-miʾati
sentences.l: And when it was the night, the ninth and the seventy after the hundred,
sentences.i: And when it was the hundred and seventy-ninth night,
sentences.n: The opening formula as before, with al-tāsiʿa, “the ninth”, feminine to agree with layla. The ئ of المائة is printed.

sentences.t: قَالَتْ بَلَغَنِي أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ السَّعِيدُأَنَّ الْعِفْرِيتَ دَهْنَشًا بْنَ شَمْهُورَشَ قَالَ لِلْعِفْرِيتَةِ مَيْمُونَةَ وَقَدِ اخْتَصَرْتُ فِي وَصْفِهَا خَوْفَ الْإِطَالَةِ
sentences.tr: qālat balaghanī ayyuhā al-maliku al-saʿīdu anna al-ʿifrīta Dahnashan ibna Shamhūrasha qāla li-al-ʿifrītati Maymūnata wa-qadi ikhtaṣartu fī waṣfihā khawfa al-iṭālati
sentences.l: She-said: It-has-reached-me, O fortunate king, that the-ifrit Dahnash son-of Shamhūrash said to-the-she-ifrit Maymūna: And-indeed I-have-abridged in describing-her (for) fear (of) the-lengthening.
sentences.i: She said: It has reached me, O fortunate king, that the ifrit Dahnash son of Shamhūrash said to the she-ifrit Maymūna, “I have cut short my description of her for fear of going on too long.”
sentences.n: Shahrazād takes up Dahnash's last words from the night before. The print runs السعيد and ان together as one word, السعيدان: read al-saʿīdu anna, “the fortunate, that”. After anna, al-ʿifrīta, “the ifrit”, is accusative, and the name beside it follows suit, printed دهنشا with the alif of the indefinite accusative, Dahnashan, as in the previous night. ibn, “son”, is written بن without its alif between two names. li-, “to”, marks the one addressed; ʿifrīta is the feminine of ʿifrīt. khawfa, “for fear of”, is an accusative of reason.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعَتْ مَيْمُونَةُ وَصْفَ تِلْكَ الصَّبِيَّةِ وَحُسْنَهَا وَجَمَالَهَا تَعَجَّبَتْ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿat Maymūnatu waṣfa tilka al-ṣabiyyati wa-ḥusnahā wa-jamālahā taʿajjabat
sentences.l: And-when Maymūna heard (the) description (of) that the-girl and-her-beauty and-her-loveliness, she-marvelled.
sentences.i: When Maymūna heard the description of that girl, of her beauty and her loveliness, she marvelled.
sentences.n: The print itself marks the shadda of تعجّبت, taʿajjabat, “she wondered, marvelled”.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهَا دَهْنَشُ وَإِنَّ أَبَا تِلْكَ الصَّبِيَّةِ مَلِكٌ جَبَّارٌ فَارِسٌ كَرَّارٌ خَوَّاضُ الْمَعَامِعِ فِى اللَّيْلِ وَالنَّهَارِ لَا يَهَابُ الْمَوْتَ وَلَا يَخَافُ الْفَوْتَ لِأَنَّهُ جَائِرٌ ظَلُومٌ وَقَاهِرٌ غَشُومٌ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahā Dahnashu wa-inna abā tilka al-ṣabiyyati malikun jabbārun fārisun karrārun khawwāḍu al-maʿāmiʿi fī al-layli wa-al-nahāri lā yahābu al-mawta wa-lā yakhāfu al-fawta li-annahu jāʾirun ẓalūmun wa-qāhirun ghashūmun
sentences.l: So-said to-her Dahnash: And-indeed (the) father (of) that the-girl (is) a-king mighty, a-horseman charging-again-and-again, a-wader-into the-din-of-battles in the-night and-the-day; not he-fears the-death and-not he-dreads the-missing-out, because-he (is) unjust, oppressive, and-subduing, tyrannous.
sentences.i: Then Dahnash said to her, “The father of that girl is a mighty king, a horseman who charges and charges again, who wades into the din of battle by night and by day; he does not fear death, nor does he dread what may slip from his grasp, for he is unjust and oppressive, a tyrant who crushes all before him.
sentences.n: Rhymed prose runs through the portrait: jabbār / karrār, al-layl / al-nahār, al-mawt / al-fawt, ẓalūm / ghashūm. The print itself marks the shadda of جبّار, كرّار and خوّاض and the fatha of المَعامع. karrār, “one who returns to the charge again and again”, and khawwāḍ, “one who wades in”, are intensive forms; maʿāmiʿ is the din and press of battle (sing. maʿmaʿa). al-fawt is “a thing passing out of reach”: he fears neither death nor loss, a jingle more than a precise thought. Dahnash resumes with wa-inna, “and indeed”, as if carrying on his account. The ئ of جائر is printed.

sentences.t: وَهُوَ صَاحِبُ جُيُوشٍ وَعَسَاكِرَ وَأَقَالِيمَ وَجَزَائِرَ وَمُدُنٍ وَدُورٍ وَاسْمُهُ الْمَلِكُ الْغَيُورُ صَاحِبُ الْجَزَائِرِ وَالْبُحُورِ وَالسَّبْعَةِ قُصُورٍ
sentences.tr: wa-huwa ṣāḥibu juyūshin wa-ʿasākira wa-aqālīma wa-jazāʾira wa-mudunin wa-dūrin wa-ismuhu al-maliku al-Ghayūru ṣāḥibu al-jazāʾiri wa-al-buḥūri wa-al-sabʿati quṣūrin
sentences.l: And-he (is) master (of) armies and-hosts and-provinces and-islands and-cities and-dwellings, and-his-name (is) the-king al-Ghayūr, lord (of) the-islands and-the-seas and-the-seven palaces.
sentences.i: He is master of armies and hosts, of provinces and islands, of cities and dwellings, and his name is King al-Ghayūr, lord of the islands and the seas and the seven palaces.
sentences.n: The rhyme now falls on -ūr: dūr / al-Ghayūr / al-buḥūr / quṣūr. The king's title repeats the one Dahnash gave in the previous night, again with al-sabʿati quṣūrin putting the article on the numeral rather than the noun. ʿasākir, aqālīm and jazāʾir are diptote plurals and take -a, not -in, after ṣāḥibu. The print itself marks the damma of مُدن; the ئ of جزائر is printed.

sentences.t: وَكَانَ يُحِبُّ ابْنَتَهُ هٰذِهِ الصَّبِيَّةَ الَّتِي وَصَفْتُهَالَكِ حُبًّا شَدِيدًا
sentences.tr: wa-kāna yuḥibbu ibnatahu hādhihi al-ṣabiyyata allatī waṣaftuhā laki ḥubban shadīdan
sentences.l: And-he-was loving his-daughter, this the-girl whom I-described-her to-you, (with) a-love intense.
sentences.i: And he loved this daughter of his, the girl I have described to you, with a fierce love.
sentences.n: The print runs وصفتها and لك together as one word, وصفتهالك: read waṣaftuhā laki, “I described her to you”, laki being feminine because Dahnash is speaking to Maymūna. The -hā repeats the antecedent of allatī, as Arabic requires: literally “whom I described her”. ḥubban shadīdan is an absolute object, “loved … with a strong love”; the print itself marks its shadda.

sentences.t: وَمِنْ مَحَبَّتِهِ لَهَا جَلَبَ أَمْوَالَ سَائِرِ الْمُلُوكِ وَبَنَى لَهَا بِذٰلِكَ سَبْعَةَ قُصُورٍ كُلُّ قَصْرٍ مِنْ جِنْسٍ مَخْصُوصٍ
sentences.tr: wa-min maḥabbatihi lahā jalaba amwāla sāʾiri al-mulūki wa-banā lahā bi-dhālika sabʿata quṣūrin kullu qaṣrin min jinsin makhṣūṣin
sentences.l: And-from his-love for-her he-brought-in (the) wealth (of) all the-kings, and-he-built for-her with-that seven palaces, every palace of a-kind particular.
sentences.i: Out of his love for her he gathered in the wealth of all the kings, and with it he built her seven palaces, each of its own particular kind.
sentences.n: sāʾir here means “all”, as often in this prose, rather than Classical “the rest of”. bi-dhālika, “with that”: bi- of the means, the wealth paying for the palaces. kullu qaṣrin … is a clause of circumstance with no linking word: “each palace (being) of …”. The ئ of سائر is printed.

sentences.t: الْقَصْرُ الْأَوَّلُ مِنَ الْبَلُّورِ وَالثَّانِي مِنَ الرُّخَامِ وَالثَّالِثُ مِنَ الْحَدِيدِ الصِّينِيِّ وَالْقَصْرُ الرَّابِعُ مِنَ الْمَعَادِنِ وَالْجَوَاهِرِ وَالْقَصْرُ الْخَامِسُ مِنَ الْخَزَفِ وَالْجَزْعِ الْمُلَوَّنِ وَالْفُصُوصِ وَالْقَصْرُ السَّادِسُ مِنَ الْفِضَّةِ وَالْقَصْرُ السَّابِعُ مِنَ الذَّهَبِ
sentences.tr: al-qaṣru al-awwalu mina al-ballūri wa-al-thānī mina al-rukhāmi wa-al-thālithu mina al-ḥadīdi al-ṣīniyyi wa-al-qaṣru al-rābiʿu mina al-maʿādini wa-al-jawāhiri wa-al-qaṣru al-khāmisu mina al-khazafi wa-al-jazʿi al-mulawwani wa-al-fuṣūṣi wa-al-qaṣru al-sādisu mina al-fiḍḍati wa-al-qaṣru al-sābiʿu mina al-dhahabi
sentences.l: The-palace the-first of the-crystal, and-the-second of the-marble, and-the-third of the-iron the-Chinese, and-the-palace the-fourth of the-metals and-the-jewels, and-the-palace the-fifth of the-glazed-ware and-the-onyx the-coloured and-the-gemstones, and-the-palace the-sixth of the-silver, and-the-palace the-seventh of the-gold.
sentences.i: The first palace was of crystal, the second of marble, the third of Chinese iron, the fourth of precious metals and jewels, the fifth of glazed ware, many-coloured onyx and gemstones, the sixth of silver and the seventh of gold.
sentences.n: “Was” is understood throughout the list. Chinese iron was reckoned a fine, hard metal. khazaf is fired and glazed earthenware; jazʿ is onyx, the banded stone; fuṣūṣ, plural of faṣṣ, are cut stones such as are set in rings. The print itself marks the shadda of البلّور, al-ballūr, “crystal”, and of الملوّن, al-mulawwan, “coloured”.

sentences.t: وَمَلَأَ السَّبْعَةَ قُصُورٍ مِنْ أَنْوَاعِ الْفَرْشِ الْفَاخِرِ مِنَ الْحَرِيرِ وَأَوَانِي الذَّهَبِ وَالْفِضَّةِ وَجَمِيعِ الْآلَاتِ مِنْ كُلِّ مَا تَحْتَاجُ إِلَيْهِ الْمُلُوكُ
sentences.tr: wa-malaʾa al-sabʿata quṣūrin min anwāʿi al-farshi al-fākhiri mina al-ḥarīri wa-awānī al-dhahabi wa-al-fiḍḍati wa-jamīʿi al-ālāti min kulli mā taḥtāju ilayhi al-mulūku
sentences.l: And-he-filled the-seven palaces with kinds (of) the-furnishing the-splendid of the-silk, and-vessels (of) the-gold and-the-silver, and-all the-implements, of everything that need it the-kings.
sentences.i: And he filled the seven palaces with every kind of splendid silken furnishing, with vessels of gold and silver, and with every appointment that kings could require.
sentences.n: malaʾa … min, “filled … with”: min marks what fills. farsh is a collective, “furnishings, carpets and cushions”, hence the singular adjective al-fākhir. iḥtāja ilā, “to need”, takes its object with ilā, so ilayhi, “(to) it”, picks up mā, “what”. The hamza of ملأ and the madda of الآلات are printed.

sentences.t: وَأَمَرَ ابْنَتَهُ أَنْ تَسْكُنَ فِي كُلِّ قَصْرٍ مُدَّةً مِنَ السَّنَةِ ثُمَّ تَنْتَقِلَ مِنْهُ إِلَى قَصْرٍ غَيْرِهِ
sentences.tr: wa-amara ibnatahu an taskuna fī kulli qaṣrin muddatan mina al-sanati thumma tantaqila minhu ilā qaṣrin ghayrihi
sentences.l: And-he-ordered his-daughter that she-dwell in every palace a-period of the-year, then she-move from-it to a-palace other-than-it.
sentences.i: And he bade his daughter live in each palace for a part of the year and then move from it to another.
sentences.n: amara here gives its order with an and the subjunctive; tantaqila is subjunctive too, still under an.

sentences.t: وَاسْمُهَا الْمَلِكَةُ بُدُورُ
sentences.tr: wa-ismuhā al-malikatu Budūru
sentences.l: And-her-name (is) the-queen Budūr.
sentences.i: Her name is Princess Budūr.
sentences.n: Budūr means “full moons”, plural of badr. al-malika is literally “the queen”; said of a king's daughter it is her royal title, and “princess” is the English for it.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا اشْتَهَرَ حُسْنُهَا وَشَاعَ فِى الْبِلَادِ ذِكْرُهَا أَرْسَلَ سَائِرُ الْمُلُوكِ إِلَى أَبِيهَا يَخْطُبُونَهَا مِنْهُ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā ishtahara ḥusnuhā wa-shāʿa fī al-bilādi dhikruhā arsala sāʾiru al-mulūki ilā abīhā yakhṭubūnahā minhu
sentences.l: And-when became-famous her-beauty and-spread in the-lands her-fame, sent all the-kings to her-father, asking-for-her-hand from-him.
sentences.i: And when her beauty grew famous and word of her spread through the lands, all the kings sent to her father to ask him for her hand.
sentences.n: The rhyme is ḥusnuhā / dhikruhā. arsala is singular because the verb comes before its subject; then yakhṭubūnahā, “they ask for her in marriage”, is plural, agreeing with the kings in sense. khaṭaba … min, “to ask for (a woman) in marriage from (her guardian)”.

sentences.t: فَشَاوَرَهَا وَرَاوَدَهَا فِي أَمْرِ الزَّوَاجِ فَكَرِهَتْ ذٰلِكَ
sentences.tr: fa-shāwarahā wa-rāwadahā fī amri al-zawāji fa-karihat dhālika
sentences.l: So-he-consulted-her and-coaxed-her in (the) matter (of) the-marriage, and-she-disliked that.
sentences.i: So he consulted her and pressed her on the matter of marriage, but she would have none of it.
sentences.n: rāwada is “to try to win someone over, to coax”; fī marks the matter in question.

sentences.t: وَقَالَتْ لِأَبِيهَا يَا وَالِدِي لَيْسَ لِي غَرَضٌ فِى الزَّوَاجِ أَبَدًا فَإِنِّي سَيِّدَةٌ وَحَاكِمَةٌ وَمَلِكَةٌ أَحْكُمُ عَلَى النَّاسِ وَلَا أُرِيدُ رَجُلًا يَحْكُمُ عَلَيَّ
sentences.tr: wa-qālat li-abīhā yā wālidī laysa lī gharaḍun fī al-zawāji abadan fa-innī sayyidatun wa-ḥākimatun wa-malikatun aḥkumu ʿalā al-nāsi wa-lā urīdu rajulan yaḥkumu ʿalayya
sentences.l: And-she-said to-her-father: O my-father, not-is to-me a-desire in the-marriage ever, for-I (am) a-mistress and-a-ruler and-a-queen; I-rule over the-people, and-not I-want a-man (who) rules over-me.
sentences.i: And she said to her father, ‘Father, I have no wish ever to marry, for I am a mistress and a ruler and a queen; I rule over people, and I want no man to rule over me.’
sentences.n: gharaḍ, “aim, wish”, with fī for the thing wished for. The print itself marks the shadda of عليّ, ʿalayya, “over me”: ḥakama ʿalā, “to rule over”. Her words turn on that verb, aḥkumu / yaḥkumu.

sentences.t: وَكُلَّمَا امْتَنَعَتْ مِنَ الزَّوَاجِ زَادَتْ رَغْبَةُ الْخُطَّابِ فِيهَا
sentences.tr: wa-kullamā imtanaʿat mina al-zawāji zādat raghbatu al-khuṭṭābi fīhā
sentences.l: And-whenever she-held-back from the-marriage, increased (the) desire (of) the-suitors for-her.
sentences.i: And the more she refused marriage, the more the suitors desired her.
sentences.n: kullamā, “whenever, every time that”. imtanaʿa min, “to hold back from, refuse”. khuṭṭāb, “suitors”, is the plural of khāṭib; the print itself marks its shadda. raghba fī, “desire for”: fī marks what is desired.

sentences.t: فَعِنْدَ ذٰلِكَ أَرْسَلَتْ جَمِيعُ مُلُوكِ جَزَائِرِ الصِّينِ الْجَوَّانِيَّةِ لِأَبِيهَا الْهَدَايَا وَالتُّحَفَ وَكَاتَبُوهُ فِي أَمْرِ زَوَاجِهَا
sentences.tr: fa-ʿinda dhālika arsalat jamīʿu mulūki jazāʾiri al-Ṣīni al-jawwāniyyati li-abīhā al-hadāyā wa-al-tuḥafa wa-kātabūhu fī amri zawājihā
sentences.l: And-at that, sent all (the) kings (of the) islands (of) China the-inner to-her-father the-gifts and-the-rarities, and-they-wrote-to-him in (the) matter (of) her-marriage.
sentences.i: Thereupon all the kings of the Inner Islands of China sent her father gifts and rarities and wrote to him about her marriage.
sentences.n: arsalat is feminine singular: a verb before a broken plural such as mulūk may agree in the feminine, and jamīʿ takes the gender of what follows it. Then kātabūhu, “they wrote to him”, is plural. al-jawwāniyya, “the inner”, a post-classical word from jawwa, “inside”, with its shadda printed; these are the islands “within the lands of China” of the previous night. li-, “to”, does the work of ilā after arsala. The ئ of جزائر is printed.

sentences.t: فَكَرَّرَ عَلَيْهَا أَبُوهَا الْمُشَاوَرَةَ فِي أَمْرِ الزَّوَاجِ مِرَارًا عَدِيدَةً فَخَالَفَتْهُ وَسَفِهَتْ عَلَيْهِ وَغَضِبَتْ مِنْهُ
sentences.tr: fa-karrara ʿalayhā abūhā al-mushāwarata fī amri al-zawāji mirāran ʿadīdatan fa-khālafathu wa-safihat ʿalayhi wa-ghaḍibat minhu
sentences.l: So-repeated to-her her-father the-consulting in (the) matter (of) the-marriage times many, and-she-opposed-him and-was-insolent toward-him and-was-angry with-him.
sentences.i: Again and again her father put the question of marriage to her, but she defied him, spoke insolently to him and grew angry with him.
sentences.n: karrara ʿalā, “to put (something) again to someone”. safiha is “to be foolish”; with ʿalā, “to behave insolently towards” someone. ghaḍiba min, “to be angry with”.

sentences.t: وَقَالَتْ لَهُ يَا أَبِي إِنْ ذَكَرْتَ لِيَ الزَّوَاجَ مَرَّةً أُخْرَى دَخَلْتُ الْبَيْتَ وَأَخَذْتُ السَّيْفَ وَغَرَزْتُ قَائِمَهُ فِى الْأَرْضِ وَأَدْخَلْتُ ذُبَابَتَهُ فِي بَطْنِي وَأَتَّكِئُ عَلَيْهِ حَتَّى يَطْلُعَ مِنْ ظَهْرِي وَأَقْتُلُ نَفْسِي
sentences.tr: wa-qālat lahu yā abī in dhakarta liya al-zawāja marratan ukhrā dakhaltu al-bayta wa-akhadhtu al-sayfa wa-gharaztu qāʾimahu fī al-arḍi wa-adkhaltu dhubābatahu fī baṭnī wa-attakiʾu ʿalayhi ḥattā yaṭlaʿa min ẓahrī wa-aqtulu nafsī
sentences.l: And-she-said to-him: O my-father, if you-mentioned to-me the-marriage another time, I-entered the-room and-took the-sword and-planted its-hilt in the-ground and-put its-point into my-belly, and-I-lean on-it until it-comes-out from my-back, and-I-kill myself.
sentences.i: And she said to him, ‘Father, if you speak to me of marriage one more time, I will go into my room, take the sword, plant its hilt in the ground, set its point to my belly and lean on it until it comes out through my back, and so kill myself.’
sentences.n: After in, “if”, the perfects dhakarta … dakhaltu … adkhaltu have future sense, as in any Arabic condition; then she slides into the imperfect, attakiʾu … aqtulu, as the threat plays out before her eyes. qāʾim al-sayf is the hilt of the sword, dhubāba its point. al-bayt here is a room of the palace rather than a house. lī takes a helping -a before the article: liya al-zawāja. The ئ of قائمه and of اتكئ is printed.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعَ أَبُوهَا مِنْهَا هٰذَا الْكَلَامَ صَارَ الضِّيَاءُ فِي وَجْهِهِ ظَلَامًا وَاحْتَرَقَ قَلْبُهُ عَلَيْهَا غَايَةَ الِاحْتِرَاقِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿa abūhā minhā hādhā al-kalāma ṣāra al-ḍiyāʾu fī wajhihi ẓalāman wa-iḥtaraqa qalbuhu ʿalayhā ghāyata al-iḥtirāqi
sentences.l: And-when her-father heard from-her this the-speech, became the-light in his-face darkness, and-burned his-heart over-her (to the) utmost (of) the-burning.
sentences.i: When her father heard these words from her, the light in his face turned to darkness, and his heart burned for her with the fiercest burning.
sentences.n: “The light in his face became darkness” is a stock phrase of the Nights: the world went black before his eyes. iḥtaraqa qalbuhu ʿalā, “his heart burned over someone”, with anxiety for her. ghāyata al-iḥtirāqi, “the utmost of burning”, is an absolute object on the same root as the verb.

sentences.t: وَخَشِيَ أَنْ تَقْتُلَ نَفْسَهَا وَحَارَ فِي أَمْرِهَا وَفِي أَمْرِ الْمُلُوكِ الَّذِينَ خَطَبُوهَا
sentences.tr: wa-khashiya an taqtula nafsahā wa-ḥāra fī amrihā wa-fī amri al-mulūki alladhīna khaṭabūhā
sentences.l: And-he-feared that she-kill herself, and-he-was-perplexed in her-affair and-in (the) affair (of) the-kings who asked-for-her-hand.
sentences.i: He feared she would kill herself, and he was at a loss what to do about her and about the kings who had asked for her hand.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهَا إِنْ كَانَ وَلَابُدَّ مِنْ عَدَمِ زَوَاجِكِ فَامْتَنِعِي مِنَ الدُّخُولِ وَالْخُرُوجِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahā in kāna wa-lā budda min ʿadami zawājiki fa-imtaniʿī mina al-dukhūli wa-al-khurūji
sentences.l: So-he-said to-her: If it-is, and-no escape from (the) absence (of) your-marrying, then-hold-back from the-going-in and-the-going-out.
sentences.i: So he said to her, ‘If it must be that you will not marry, then keep yourself from going in and out.’
sentences.n: in kāna wa-lā budda min, “if it is so, and there is no help for it”, is a set phrase; the print sets lā budda as one word, ولابد. ʿadam, “absence, non-being”, makes a noun of the negative: “the not-marrying of you”. al-dukhūl wa-al-khurūj, “going in and coming out”, is moving freely about: he is confining her.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ أَبَاهَا أَدْخَلَهَا الْبَيْتَ وَحَجَبَهَا فِيهِ وَرَسَمَ عَلَيْهَا عَشَرَةَ عَجَائِزَ قَهْرَمَانَاتٍ وَمَنَعَهَا مِنْ أَنْ تَظْهَرَ إِلَى السَّبْعِ قُصُورٍ
sentences.tr: thumma inna abāhā adkhalahā al-bayta wa-ḥajabahā fīhi wa-rasama ʿalayhā ʿasharata ʿajāʾiza qahramānātin wa-manaʿahā min an taẓhara ilā al-sabʿi quṣūrin
sentences.l: Then indeed her-father put-her-into the-room and-secluded-her in-it, and-set over-her ten old-women stewardesses, and-kept-her from that she-come-out to the-seven palaces.
sentences.i: Then her father shut her up in her room and kept her secluded there; he set ten old women, stewardesses, to watch over her, and forbade her to show herself in the seven palaces.
sentences.n: rasama ʿalā, “to give orders concerning”, here “to set (keepers) over”. qahramāna, from Persian, is the stewardess of a great household. Both numerals go against the Classical rule, which takes the form without -a before a feminine noun and the form with -a before a masculine one: ʿashru ʿajāʾiza, al-quṣūru al-sabʿatu. The print has ʿashara with the feminine ʿajāʾiz, and al-sabʿ, without -a, with the masculine quṣūr, where earlier in the night it said al-sabʿa quṣūr: in the spoken language the gender of numerals had come loose. ẓahara ilā, “to come out into”. The ئ of عجائز is printed.

sentences.t: وَأَظْهَرَ أَنَّهُ غَضْبَانُ عَلَيْهَا وَأَرْسَلَ كَاتَبَ الْمُلُوكَ جَمِيعَهُمْ وَأَعْلَمَهُمْ أَنَّهَا أُصِيبَتْ بِجُنُونٍ فِي عَقْلِهَا وَلَهَا الْآنَ سَنَةٌ وَهِيَ مَحْجُوبَةٌ
sentences.tr: wa-aẓhara annahu ghaḍbānu ʿalayhā wa-arsala kātaba al-mulūka jamīʿahum wa-aʿlamahum annahā uṣībat bi-junūnin fī ʿaqlihā wa-lahā al-āna sanatun wa-hiya maḥjūbatun
sentences.l: And-he-made-it-appear that-he (was) angry with-her, and-he-sent, wrote-to the-kings all-of-them, and-informed-them that-she had-been-struck with madness in her-mind, and to-her now a-year and-she (is) secluded.
sentences.i: He let it be seen that he was angry with her, and he sent letters to all the kings, informing them that she had been stricken with madness and had now been kept in seclusion for a year.”
sentences.n: wa-arsala kātaba al-mulūka, “and he sent, wrote to the kings”, sets two verbs side by side with no “and” between them. That may be the loose run of the storytelling, or a و may have dropped out before كاتب; one could also read kātiba al-mulūki, “he sent the kings' scribe”, but that makes poorer sense. The print is kept and read the first way. ghaḍbān, “angry”, is diptote and takes no tanwīn. uṣībat bi-, “was struck with”: bi- marks the affliction. wa-lahā al-āna sanatun, “and to her is now a year”, is the Arabic for “for a year now”. The madda of الآن is printed.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ الْعِفْرِيتَ دَهْنَشَ قَالَ لِلْعِفْرِيتَةِ مَيْمُونَةَ وَأَنَا أَرُوحُ إِلَيْهَا يَا سَيِّدَتِي فِي كُلِّ لَيْلَةٍ فَأَنْظُرُهَا وَأَتَمَلَّى بِوَجْهِهَا وَأُقَبِّلُهَا وَهِيَ نَائِمَةٌ بَيْنَ عَيْنَيْهَا
sentences.tr: thumma inna al-ʿifrīta Dahnasha qāla li-al-ʿifrītati Maymūnata wa-anā arūḥu ilayhā yā sayyidatī fī kulli laylatin fa-anẓuruhā wa-atamallā bi-wajhihā wa-uqabbiluhā wa-hiya nāʾimatun bayna ʿaynayhā
sentences.l: Then indeed the-ifrit Dahnash said to-the-she-ifrit Maymūna: And-I, I-go to-her, O my-lady, in every night, and-I-look-at-her and-I-feast-(my-eyes) on-her-face and-I-kiss-her, and-she (is) sleeping, between her-two-eyes.
sentences.i: Then the ifrit Dahnash said to the she-ifrit Maymūna, “I go to her every night, my lady, and gaze at her, and feast my eyes on her face, and kiss her between the eyes as she sleeps.
sentences.n: thumma inna, “then”, is the narrator's usual way of moving the story on; inna makes al-ʿifrīta accusative, and the name after it, Dahnasha, follows in the accusative, here without the alif of -an, so treated as a diptote (contrast دهنشا a few lines below). rāḥa ilā, “to go to”, is the everyday verb of the later language. tamallā bi-, “to enjoy something at length, take one's fill of”: bi- marks what is enjoyed, here her face. wa-hiya nāʾimatun, “while she is asleep”, is a circumstantial clause, and bayna ʿaynayhā, “between her two eyes”, says where the kiss falls, on the brow. The shaddas of واتملّى and واقبّلها are printed, and so is the ئ of نائمة.

sentences.t: وَمِنْ مَحَبَّتِي فِيهَا لَا أَضُرُّهَا وَلَا أُوذِيهَا وَلَا أَرْكَبُهَا لِأَنَّ شَبَابَهَا مَلِيحٌ وَجَمَالَهَا بَارِعٌ كُلُّ مَنْ رَآهَا يَغَارُ عَلَيْهَا مِنْ نَفْسِهِ
sentences.tr: wa-min maḥabbatī fīhā lā aḍurruhā wa-lā ūdhīhā wa-lā arkabuhā li-anna shabābahā malīḥun wa-jamālahā bāriʿun kullu man raʾāhā yaghāru ʿalayhā min nafsihi
sentences.l: And-from my-love in-her, not I-harm-her and-not I-hurt-her and-not I-mount-her, because her-youth (is) lovely and-her-beauty surpassing; every who saw-her is-jealous over-her from himself.
sentences.i: And for the love I bear her I do her no harm, I do not hurt her, and I do not mount her, for her youth is so lovely and her beauty so surpassing that whoever sees her is jealous over her even of himself.
sentences.n: maḥabbatī fīhā, “my love in her”: maḥabba fī is a common way of saying love for someone. rakiba, “to ride, mount”, is used plainly of a man taking a woman; Dahnash means he has not lain with her. li-anna, “because”, makes both shabābahā and jamālahā accusative. kullu man raʾāhā yaghāru ʿalayhā min nafsihi, “everyone who sees her is jealous over her of his own self”: ghāra ʿalā is to be jealous for or over a woman, and min nafsihi, “of himself”, is a lover's conceit, that he would grudge her even to his own eyes. The shadda of اضرّها is printed, and so is the آ of رآها.

sentences.t: وَأَقْسَمْتُ عَلَيْكِ يَاسَيِّدَتِي أَنْ تَرْجِعِي مَعِي وَتَنْظُرِي حُسْنَهَا وَجَمَالَهَا وَقَدَّهَا وَاعْتِدَالَهَا
sentences.tr: wa-aqsamtu ʿalayki yā sayyidatī an tarjiʿī maʿī wa-tanẓurī ḥusnahā wa-jamālahā wa-qaddahā wa-iʿtidālahā
sentences.l: And-I-have-sworn upon-you, O-my-lady, that you-return with-me and-look-at her-loveliness and-her-beauty and-her-stature and-her-straightness.
sentences.i: I adjure you, my lady, to come back with me and see her loveliness and her beauty, her figure and her grace of form.
sentences.n: aqsamtu ʿalayki an, “I have sworn upon you that”, is the formula of earnest entreaty, “I adjure you to”; the perfect is performative, the oath made in the saying. The print runs يا سيدتي together as ياسيدتي; the spacing is kept, read yā sayyidatī. qadd is a person's stature, and iʿtidāl the straight, well-proportioned build that goes with it: a stock pair in praise of beauty. The shadda of وقدّها is printed.

sentences.t: وَبَعْدَ هٰذَا إِنْ شِئْتِ أَنْ تُعَاتِبِينِي أَوْتَأْسِرِينِي فَافْعَلِي فَإِنَّ الْأَمْرَ أَمْرُكِ وَالنَّهْيَ نَهْيُكِ
sentences.tr: wa-baʿda hādhā in shiʾti an tuʿātibīnī aw taʾsirīnī fa-ifʿalī fa-inna al-amra amruki wa-al-nahya nahyuki
sentences.l: And-after this, if you-wish to reproach-me or take-me-captive, then-do; for indeed the-command (is) your-command and-the-forbidding your-forbidding.
sentences.i: After that, if you wish to reproach me or make me your captive, do so; for yours is the command and yours the prohibition.”
sentences.n: The print runs او تأسريني together as اوتأسريني; the spacing is kept, read aw taʾsirīnī, “or take me captive”, from asara, “to bind, take prisoner”. ʿātaba, “to reproach, upbraid”, Form III. al-amru amruki wa-al-nahyu nahyuki, “the command is your command and the forbidding is your forbidding”, is the stock formula of submission, rhyming on -ruki / -yuki; al-nahya is accusative because inna governs both halves. The ئ of شئت and the أ of تأسريني are printed.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ الْعِفْرِيتَ دَهْنَشًا أَطْرَقَ بِرَأْسِهِ إِلَى الْأَرْضِ وَخَفَضَ أَجْنِحَتَهُ إِلَى الْأَرْضِ
sentences.tr: thumma inna al-ʿifrīta Dahnashan aṭraqa bi-raʾsihi ilā al-arḍi wa-khafaḍa ajniḥatahu ilā al-arḍi
sentences.l: Then indeed the-ifrit Dahnash lowered with-his-head to the-ground, and-lowered his-wings to the-ground.
sentences.i: Then the ifrit Dahnash bowed his head to the ground and lowered his wings to the ground.
sentences.n: Here the print spells the name دهنشا, with the alif of the indefinite accusative, Dahnashan, as in the previous night. aṭraqa bi-raʾsihi, “to bow the head”: aṭraqa alone is to lower the eyes and fall silent, and bi- brings in what is lowered. ajniḥa is a plural of janāḥ, “wing”; the jinn of the Nights fly on wings. The أ of برأسه is printed.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ لَهُ الْعِفْرِيتَةُ مَيْمُونَةُ بَعْدَ أَنْ ضِحِكَتْ مِنْ كَلَامِهِ وَبَصَقَتْ فِي وَجْهِهِ
sentences.tr: fa-qālat lahu al-ʿifrītatu Maymūnatu baʿda an ḍiḥikat min kalāmihi wa-baṣaqat fī wajhihi
sentences.l: And-said to-him the-she-ifrit Maymūna, after she-laughed at his-speech and-spat in his-face:
sentences.i: The she-ifrit Maymūna laughed at what he had said, spat in his face, and said to him,
sentences.n: The kasra on the first letter of ضِحكت is printed: it records the spoken pronunciation ḍiḥikat, where Classical has ḍaḥikat, and the pointing follows it. ḍaḥika min, “to laugh at”: min marks what is laughed at. Her words follow in the next sentence.

sentences.t: أَيْشْ هٰذِهِ الْبِنْتُ الَّتِي تَقُولُ عَنْهَا فَمَا هِيَ إِلَّا قَوَّارَةُ الْبَوْلِ أُفُوهْ أُفُوهْ
sentences.tr: aysh hādhihi al-bintu allatī taqūlu ʿanhā fa-mā hiya illā qawwāratu al-bawli ufūh ufūh
sentences.l: What (is) this the-girl that you-speak about-her? For not she (is) except (the) jar (of) the-urine. Ugh, ugh!
sentences.i: “What is this girl you talk about? She is nothing but a piss-pot. Ugh, ugh!
sentences.n: The print has اقوه twice, a misprint for افوه, corrected here; the dot of the fāʾ has been doubled in setting. ufūh, “ugh!”, is an interjection of disgust, akin to uff, and the same form appears in the tale of ʿAjīb (Night 23); its exact pronunciation is not certain. aysh, “what”, is colloquial, contracted from ayyu shayʾin, “which thing”. mā hiya illā, “she is not but”, that is, “she is nothing but”. qawwāra is not in the Classical dictionaries in this sense, and the pointing is a guess; it seems to be a spoken form of qārūra, the glass flask in which urine was carried to the physician to be inspected, so qawwāratu al-bawli is a urine flask, a chamber pot: Maymūna is calling the princess a vessel for piss.

sentences.t: وَاللّٰهِ إِنِّي حَسِبْتُ أَنَّ مَعَكَ أَمْرًا عَجِيبًا أَوْ خَبَرًا غَرِيبًا يَا مَلْعُونُ
sentences.tr: wa-Allāhi innī ḥasibtu anna maʿaka amran ʿajīban aw khabaran gharīban yā malʿūnu
sentences.l: By-God, indeed-I thought that with-you (was) a-matter wondrous or a-tiding strange, O cursed-one!
sentences.i: By God, I thought you had something wondrous to show, or some strange news, you damned wretch!
sentences.n: wa-Allāhi, “by God”: wa- of oath, with the genitive. ḥasiba, “to think, suppose”. maʿaka, “with you”, is “you have”. The rhyme falls on ʿajīban / gharīban. malʿūn, “cursed”, passive participle of laʿana, is a common term of abuse.

sentences.t: فَكَيْفَ لَوْ رَأَيْتَ مَعْشُوقَتِي
sentences.tr: fa-kayfa law raʾayta maʿshūqatī
sentences.l: So-how (would it be) if you-saw my-beloved?
sentences.i: What then if you were to see my beloved?
sentences.n: fa-kayfa law, “so how if”, with the rest left unsaid: “how would you be if you saw …”. maʿshūqatī, “my beloved”, has the feminine ending, though Maymūna's beloved is a youth and a few lines below she says maʿshūqī; the feminine may be a slip of the print or loose usage, and it is kept as printed. maʿshūq, passive participle of ʿashiqa, “to love passionately”, is “the one loved”. The أ of رأيت is printed.

sentences.t: إِنِّي رَأَيْتُ إِنْسَانًا فِي هٰذِهِ اللَّيْلَةِ لَوْ رَأَيْتَهُ وَلَوْ فِى الْمَنَامِ لَانْفَلَجْتَ عَلَيْهِ وَسَالَتْ رِيَالَتُكَ
sentences.tr: innī raʾaytu insānan fī hādhihi al-laylati law raʾaytahu wa-law fī al-manāmi la-infalajta ʿalayhi wa-sālat riyālatuka
sentences.l: Indeed-I saw a-human in this the-night; if you-saw-him, even-if in the-sleep, surely-you-would-be-palsied over-him and-would-flow your-drool.
sentences.i: Tonight I saw a human being such that, if you saw him even in a dream, you would be struck with palsy over him and your drool would run.”
sentences.n: The print has ربالتك, a misprint for ريالتك, corrected here: the dots of yāʾ have become the one dot of bāʾ. riyāla, “slaver, drool”, is the spoken form of Classical riyāl, the spittle that runs from the mouth. law … la-, “if … surely”: la- opens the answer to an unreal condition. wa-law fī al-manāmi, “even in sleep”, that is, in a dream. infalaja, “to be struck with palsy”, Form VII of the root of fālij, “hemiplegia”, is a spoken form; Classical says fulija. ʿalayhi, “over him”, “because of him”. The print writes في here as فى. The أ of both رأيت and رأيته is printed.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهَا دَهْنَشُ وَمَا حِكَايَةُ هٰذَا الْغُلَامِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahā Dahnashu wa-mā ḥikāyatu hādhā al-ghulāmi
sentences.l: And-said to-her Dahnash: And-what (is the) story (of) this the-youth?
sentences.i: Dahnash said to her, “And what is the story of this youth?”
sentences.n: wa-mā, “and what”: the wa- picks up her words, as English “and” does in a question. ghulām, “youth, lad”, is a young man not yet fully grown.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ لَهُ اعْلَمْ يَا دَهْنَشُ أَنَّ هٰذَا الْغُلَامَ قَدْ جَرَى لَهُ مِثْلُ مَا جَرَى لِمَعْشُوقَتِكَ الَّتِي ذَكَرْتَهَا
sentences.tr: fa-qālat lahu iʿlam yā Dahnashu anna hādhā al-ghulāma qad jarā lahu mithlu mā jarā li-maʿshūqatika allatī dhakartahā
sentences.l: And-she-said to-him: Know, O Dahnash, that this the-youth, indeed happened to-him (the) like (of) what happened to-your-beloved whom you-mentioned.
sentences.i: She said to him, “Know, Dahnash, that the same thing has befallen this youth as befell your beloved whom you spoke of.
sentences.n: jarā li-, “to happen to, befall”: li- marks the one it befalls. hādhā al-ghulāma is put first after anna and then picked up by lahu, “to him”: “this youth, there has happened to him”. What befell the princess, as Dahnash told it, was her refusal to marry.

sentences.t: وَأَمَرَهُ أَبُوهُ بِالزَّوَاجِ مِرَارًا عَدِيدَةً فَأَبَي فَلَمَّا خَالَفَ أَبَاهُ غَضِبَ عَلَيْهِ وَسَجَنَهُ فِى الْبُرْجِ الَّذِي أَنَا سَاكِنَةٌ فِيهِ
sentences.tr: wa-amarahu abūhu bi-al-zawāji mirāran ʿadīdatan fa-abā fa-lammā khālafa abāhu ghaḍiba ʿalayhi wa-sajanahu fī al-burji alladhī anā sākinatun fīhi
sentences.l: And-ordered-him his-father to-the-marrying times numerous, and-he-refused; and-when he-opposed his-father, he-grew-angry with-him and-imprisoned-him in the-tower which I (am) dwelling in-it.
sentences.i: His father ordered him many times to marry, and he refused; and when he defied his father, his father grew angry with him and shut him up in the tower where I live.
sentences.n: The print has فلبي, a misprint for فابي, corrected here: lām has been set for alif; the final ي is the print's usual spelling of alif maqṣūra, read fa-abā. The sense needs a refusal, fa-abā, “and he refused”; read as fa-labbā, “and he complied”, the word would contradict the next clause. amara bi-, “to order (someone) to do”: the verb takes bi- before the thing ordered, here al-zawāj, “marriage”. mirāran ʿadīdatan, “many times”, adverbial accusative. The subject changes without warning: it is the father who grows angry (ghaḍiba ʿalayhi) and imprisons him. alladhī anā sākinatun fīhi, “which I am living in”: the fīhi picks up the relative, as Arabic requires. The print writes في here as فى.

sentences.t: فَطَلَعْتُ فِي هٰذِهِ اللَّيْلَةِ فَرَأَيْتُهُ
sentences.tr: fa-ṭalaʿtu fī hādhihi al-laylati fa-raʾaytuhu
sentences.l: And-I-went-up in this the-night and-I-saw-him.
sentences.i: Tonight I came up and saw him.”
sentences.n: ṭalaʿa, “to go up, come up”: she came up into the tower room where the youth lies. The أ of فرأيته is printed.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهَا دَهْنَشُ يَا سَيِّدَتِي أَرِينِي هٰذَا الْغُلَامَ لِأَنْظُرَ هَلْ هُوَ أَحْسَنُ مِنْ مَعْشُوقَتِي الْمَلِكَةِ بُدُورَ أَمْ لَا لِأَنِّي مَا أَظُنُّ أَنْ يُوجَدَ فِي هٰذَا الزَّمَانِ مِثْلُ مَعْشُوقَتِي
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahā Dahnashu yā sayyidatī arīnī hādhā al-ghulāma li-anẓura hal huwa aḥsanu min maʿshūqatī al-malikati Budūra am lā li-annī mā aẓunnu an yūjada fī hādhā al-zamāni mithlu maʿshūqatī
sentences.l: And-said to-her Dahnash: O my-lady, show-me this the-youth, that-I-may-see whether he (is) more-beautiful than my-beloved the-queen Budūr or not, because-I not I-think that is-found in this the-time (the) like (of) my-beloved.
sentences.i: Dahnash said to her, “My lady, show me this youth, so that I may see whether he is more beautiful than my beloved, Princess Budūr, or not; for I do not think that in this age there is any to equal my beloved.”
sentences.n: arīnī, “show me”, the feminine imperative of arā, Form IV of raʾā, “to see”, with -nī, “me”. li-anẓura, “so that I may look”: li- of purpose, with the subjunctive. aḥsanu min, “more beautiful than”. al-malika, literally “the queen”, is used of a king's daughter, so “Princess”; the name Budūr, “full moons”, is diptote here. mā aẓunnu an yūjada, “I do not think that there is found”: yūjadu, “is found”, is the usual later way of saying “there exists”. Middle Arabic negates the imperfect with mā where Classical prefers lā.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ لَهُ الْعِفْرِيتَةُ تَكْذِبُ يَا مَلْعُونُ يَا أَنْحَسَ الْمَرَدَةِ وَأَحْقَرَ الشَّيَاطِينِ
sentences.tr: fa-qālat lahu al-ʿifrītatu takdhibu yā malʿūnu yā anḥasa al-maradati wa-aḥqara al-shayāṭīni
sentences.l: And-said to-him the-she-ifrit: You-lie, O cursed-one, O most-ill-omened (of) the-rebel-jinn and-most-contemptible (of) the-devils!
sentences.i: The she-ifrit said to him, “You lie, you damned wretch, you most ill-starred of the rebel jinn and vilest of devils!
sentences.n: takdhibu, “you lie”, the plain imperfect, in the present: “you are lying”. anḥas, “most ill-omened”, and aḥqar, “most contemptible”, are elatives, accusative because each heads a vocative phrase with a genitive after it. marada, plural of mārid, are the rebellious jinn; shayāṭīn, plural of shayṭān, “devil”.

sentences.t: فَأَنَا أَتَحَقَّقُ أَنَّهُ لَا يُوجَدُ لِمَعْشُوقِي مَثِيلٌ فِي هٰذِهِ الدِّيَارِ
sentences.tr: fa-anā ataḥaqqaqu annahu lā yūjadu li-maʿshūqī mathīlun fī hādhihi al-diyāri
sentences.l: For-I, I-am-certain that-it (is), not is-found for-my-beloved an-equal in these the-lands.
sentences.i: For I know for certain that there is none to equal my beloved in all these lands.”
sentences.n: taḥaqqaqa, “to make sure, be certain of”, Form V of the root of ḥaqq, “truth”. annahu, “that it (is)”: the -hu is the pronoun of the fact, introducing the clause after it. li-maʿshūqī, “for my beloved”, here masculine. diyār, “abodes, lands”, plural of dār.

sentences.t: وَأَدْرَكَ شَهْرَزَادَ الصَّبَاحُ فَسَكَتَتْ عَنِ الْكَلَامِ الْمُبَاحِ
sentences.tr: wa-adraka Shahrazāda al-ṣabāḥu fa-sakatat ʿani al-kalāmi al-mubāḥi
sentences.l: And the-morning overtook Shahrazād, and-she-fell-silent from the-permitted speech.
sentences.i: And morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent from the speech allowed her.
sentences.n: The closing formula, as at the end of every night.
